s:
Historians have long debated the extent to which the arrival of movable-type printing in Europe in the fifteenth century transformed the societies that adopted it. One of its less obvious effects concerned language itself. Before printing, much scholarly and religious writing circulated in Latin, a language shared by educated elites across the continent but understood by relatively few ordinary people. Printers, however, were commercial actors who needed to sell their products, and the market for Latin books was limited. As a result, they increasingly turned to the vernacular languages spoken by the wider population. This shift had consequences that no individual printer intended. Because a printed book could reach readers in many different regions, printers had an incentive to choose spellings and forms that would be understood as widely as possible. Over time, such choices helped to stabilise particular varieties of a language, which came to be regarded as standard, while regional dialects that rarely appeared in print gained less prestige. Some scholars argue that this process contributed to a growing sense of shared identity among people who read the same language, even if they would never meet one another. Others caution against overstating the role of technology, pointing out that literacy remained limited for centuries and that political and religious developments also shaped linguistic change.

Which of the following could be the best title for the passage?
c: Printing and the Unplanned Standardisation of Languages
The Decline of Latin as the Language of Religion
Why Printers Became the Most Powerful Political Leaders of Europe
Regional Dialects and the Rapid Spread of Literacy
a: Parça, matbaacıların ticari kaygılarla yerel dillere yönelmesinin, kimsenin amaçlamadığı biçimde belirli dil türlerini standartlaştırdığını anlatıyor.

A placebo is a treatment with no active therapeutic ingredient, such as a sugar pill or an injection of saline solution. In clinical trials, placebos are given to a control group so that researchers can determine whether a new drug produces benefits beyond those that arise simply from receiving treatment. Yet the improvements observed in placebo groups are frequently substantial, particularly for conditions such as pain, nausea and fatigue, in which subjective experience plays an important role. Explanations for this placebo response vary. Expectation is clearly important: patients who believe they are receiving effective care may experience genuine changes in the way the brain processes signals of discomfort. Conditioning may also contribute, since a body that has repeatedly associated a pill with relief can begin to respond to the act of taking a pill itself. s:
Public concern about microplastics, the tiny plastic fragments less than five millimetres in size, has focused largely on the oceans. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that agricultural soils may be at least as heavily contaminated. Microplastics reach farmland through several routes. Sewage sludge, which is widely spread on fields as fertiliser, often contains synthetic fibres released from washing clothes. Thin plastic films used to cover crops and retain moisture can break down into fragments if they are not fully removed after harvest, and plastic debris may also be carried by wind and irrigation water. Once in the soil, these particles do not simply remain inert. Experiments indicate that they can alter soil structure, affecting how water drains and how air circulates around plant roots. Some studies have also reported changes in the activity of earthworms and microorganisms, which perform essential roles in decomposing organic matter and recycling nutrients. Whether such effects ultimately reduce crop yields is less clear, as results have varied considerably depending on the type, shape and concentration of the plastic involved. A further concern is that microplastics may act as carriers for other pollutants, such as pesticides, which can bind to their surfaces. Because removing plastic from soil on a large scale is practically impossible, many specialists conclude that the most realistic strategy is to limit how much enters it in the first place.

The passage is mainly about ----.
c: how microplastics enter farmland and how they may affect it
why ocean pollution has attracted so much public attention
techniques that farmers use to remove plastics from fields
the role of earthworms in raising agricultural productivity
a: Parça mikroplastiklerin tarım topraklarına hangi yollarla ulaştığını ve toprak yapısı, canlılar ve diğer kirleticiler üzerindeki olası etkilerini ele alıyor.

s:
Traditional economic theory assumes that people make choices by carefully weighing costs and benefits. If this were entirely true, the way options are presented would make little difference, provided that the options themselves remain the same. Research in behavioural economics, however, has repeatedly shown that presentation matters a great deal. One of the most robust findings concerns default options, that is, the outcome that occurs if a person takes no action. When employees are automatically enrolled in a retirement savings plan and must actively choose to leave it, participation tends to be far higher than when they must actively choose to join. The underlying options are identical in both cases; only the default differs. Several explanations have been proposed. Changing a default requires effort, however small, and people tend to postpone decisions that seem complicated. Defaults may also be interpreted as implicit recommendations, signalling what the designer of the system considers sensible. In addition, people often feel more responsible for the consequences of an action than for those of inaction. Such insights have encouraged governments and organisations to design defaults deliberately in order to promote desirable behaviour. Critics, however, warn that this practice raises ethical questions. Even if individuals remain free to opt out, those who set defaults are exercising considerable influence, and their judgement of what is desirable may not coincide with the interests of everyone affected.

According to the passage, the retirement savings example demonstrates that ----.
c: behaviour can change even when the available choices stay the same
employees generally prefer plans that require an active choice
traditional theory accurately predicts participation in such plans
most people are unwilling to save any money for their retirement
a: Parçada iki durumda da seçeneklerin aynı olduğu, yalnızca varsayılanın değiştiği ('only the default differs') ve buna rağmen katılımın çok farklı olduğu vurgulanıyor.

s:
The oceans absorb a substantial share of the carbon dioxide that human activities release into the atmosphere. In one sense this is beneficial, since it slows the rate at which the gas accumulates in the air and warms the planet. The benefit, however, comes at a cost. When carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, gradually lowering the water's pH in a process known as ocean acidification. Although seawater remains slightly alkaline overall, even modest chemical changes can have significant biological consequences. Many marine organisms, including corals, oysters and certain types of plankton, build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate. Acidification reduces the availability of the carbonate ions they require, forcing them to expend more energy on construction and, in extreme cases, causing existing structures to dissolve. The effects are unlikely to be confined to these species. Coral reefs provide habitat for a remarkable diversity of marine life, and some forms of plankton lie at the base of food webs that ultimately support commercial fisheries. Researchers stress, however, that responses vary between species, and that some organisms appear more resilient than others. Acidification also interacts with other pressures, such as rising water temperatures and pollution, making its precise impact difficult to isolate. What seems clear is that reducing emissions remains the only way to address the problem at its source.

According to the passage, the absorption of carbon dioxide by the oceans ----.
c: has both a positive and a negative side
has made seawater acidic rather than alkaline
is beneficial for organisms that build shells
a: Parçada emilimin gazın havada birikmesini yavaşlattığı için yararlı olduğu, ancak 'comes at a cost' denilerek okyanus asitlenmesine yol açtığı anlatılıyor.

s:
For several decades, it was widely claimed that speaking two languages offers cognitive advantages extending well beyond language itself. According to this view, bilingual people constantly suppress one language while using the other, and this regular mental exercise strengthens so-called executive functions, such as the ability to ignore distractions and switch between tasks. Early studies appeared to support the idea, reporting that bilingual children outperformed their monolingual peers on certain tests of attention and control. In recent years, however, the bilingual advantage has become one of the more contested topics in cognitive science. Some large-scale studies have failed to replicate the earlier findings, and critics have pointed out that many of the original experiments involved small samples. They have also noted that bilingual and monolingual groups may differ in other respects, including education, income and immigration history, any of which could influence test performance. Furthermore, there is evidence that studies reporting positive results were more likely to be published than those reporting none, which may have given a distorted impression of the overall evidence. Defenders of the hypothesis respond that bilingualism is not a single experience: the age at which languages are learned and how often each is used vary enormously, and advantages may appear only under specific conditions. The debate remains unresolved. What is not in dispute is that learning another language brings considerable social, cultural and practical benefits.

The passage mainly discusses ----.
c: a once popular claim about bilingualism that is now questioned
methods for teaching a second language to young children
the reasons why bilingual people tend to earn higher incomes than others
the social benefits of learning a foreign language at school
a: Parça, iki dilliliğin bilişsel üstünlük sağladığı yönündeki eskiden yaygın görüşün bugün nasıl tartışmalı hâle geldiğini anlatıyor.

Defenders of the hypothesis respond that bilingualism is not a single experience: the age at which languages are learned and how often each is used vary enormously, and advantages may appear only under specific conditions. The debate remains unresolved. What is not in dispute is that learning another language brings considerable social, cultural and practical benefits.

s:
Antibiotics transformed medicine in the twentieth century, turning many once-deadly bacterial infections into easily treatable conditions. Their effectiveness, however, is threatened by a process that is, in essence, evolution in action. Within any large population of bacteria, a few individuals may carry genetic variations that allow them to survive exposure to a particular drug. When an antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, these resistant individuals face less competition and can multiply. Bacteria can also exchange genetic material directly, meaning that resistance may spread not only from one generation to the next but also between different species. Human practices have greatly accelerated this natural process. Antibiotics are sometimes prescribed for viral infections, against which they are entirely useless, and patients may stop taking them as soon as they feel better rather than following the course their doctor recommended. In many countries, large quantities are also used in livestock farming, sometimes to promote growth rather than to treat disease. Each unnecessary use creates further opportunities for resistant strains to emerge. Developing new antibiotics might seem an obvious response, but relatively few have reached the market in recent decades. Research is expensive and uncertain, and because new drugs are likely to be held in reserve for the most serious cases, the prospect of commercial returns is limited. Consequently, many experts argue that preserving the effectiveness of existing antibiotics is at least as important as discovering new ones.

According to the passage, resistant bacteria multiply after antibiotic treatment because ----.
c: the drug removes many of the susceptible bacteria they compete with
the antibiotic itself causes them to develop entirely new genetic variations
they receive useful genetic material directly from the drug
they are protected by viruses that the drug cannot affect
a: Parçada antibiyotik duyarlı bakterileri öldürünce dirençli olanların 'face less competition and can multiply' olduğu belirtiliyor.

s:
The name 'Silk Road' suggests a single route along which silk travelled from China to the Mediterranean. In reality, the term, which was coined only in the nineteenth century, refers to a shifting network of overland and maritime routes that linked Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe over many centuries. Few merchants travelled its entire length. Instead, goods typically passed through many hands, being exchanged at markets and oasis towns where traders from different regions met. Silk was indeed an important commodity, but it was only one of many; spices, textiles, metals, ceramics, horses and paper also moved along these routes in various directions. Historians increasingly emphasise that the exchange of goods was accompanied by an exchange of ideas, technologies and beliefs. Religious traditions spread through the activities of merchants and travelling teachers, while techniques such as papermaking gradually became known far from their places of origin. Agricultural products, musical instruments and artistic styles similarly crossed cultural boundaries. Not all exchanges were beneficial, however. The same networks that carried goods and knowledge could also transmit infectious diseases, sometimes with devastating effects on distant populations. For these reasons, many scholars now prefer to regard the Silk Road less as a trade route than as a framework for understanding how societies across Eurasia were connected long before the modern era of globalisation.

According to the passage, the name 'Silk Road' is somewhat misleading because ----.
c: it implies a single route and a single main product
silk was rarely traded between China and Europe
it was invented by merchants wishing to hide their routes
the routes it describes were used for a relatively short period
a: Ad tek bir yolu ve ipeği çağrıştırıyor; oysa parçaya göre söz konusu olan değişken bir yollar ağıdır ve ipek pek çok maldan yalnızca biridir.

s:
The human digestive system is home to trillions of microorganisms, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Once viewed mainly as passive passengers, these bacteria, fungi and other microbes are now recognised as active participants in human physiology. They help to break down dietary fibre that human enzymes cannot digest, producing compounds that nourish the cells lining the intestine. They also contribute to the development and regulation of the immune system and may compete with harmful organisms for space and resources. Because the composition of the microbiome differs considerably from one person to another, researchers have sought to link particular microbial patterns to conditions ranging from obesity to inflammatory bowel disease. Some studies have even suggested connections with mood and behaviour, through what is sometimes called the gut-brain axis. Such findings have generated considerable public enthusiasm, as well as a growing market for probiotic supplements. Scientists, however, frequently urge caution. Many of the most striking results come from experiments on mice, which do not always translate to humans. Moreover, an association between a certain microbiome and a disease does not reveal which causes which: the condition itself, or the medications used to treat it, may alter the microbial community. Diet appears to be one of the strongest influences on the microbiome, and a varied diet rich in plant foods is often associated with greater microbial diversity, although what constitutes an ideal microbiome remains uncertain.

It is stated in the passage that the gut microbiome ----.
c: helps the body make use of fibre it could not otherwise digest
consists entirely of bacteria that are harmful to humans
is nearly identical in composition in all healthy adults and children
weakens the immune system by competing with useful cells
a: Parçada mikropların insan enzimlerinin sindiremediği lifleri parçaladığı ve bağırsak hücrelerini besleyen bileşikler ürettiği belirtiliyor.

s:
Fears that machines will cause mass unemployment are almost as old as industrialisation itself. In the early nineteenth century, some textile workers in England destroyed machinery they believed threatened their livelihoods, and similar anxieties have resurfaced with each major wave of technological change. Historically, however, the predicted collapse in employment has not materialised. Although specific occupations have declined, new kinds of work have emerged, often in sectors scarcely imagined beforehand. Economists generally explain this pattern by noting that technology does not only replace human labour; it also raises productivity, lowers prices and creates demand for new goods and services. Whether this historical pattern will continue is the subject of considerable debate. Earlier waves of automation mostly affected routine physical tasks, whereas advances in computing and artificial intelligence increasingly allow machines to perform cognitive tasks once thought to require human judgement. Some analysts argue that this difference is one of degree rather than kind and that labour markets will adjust as before. Others contend that the pace and breadth of current change may leave many workers unable to retrain quickly enough. Even optimists usually concede that the transition is likely to be uneven. The benefits of new technology may accrue mainly to those with the skills to use it, while workers whose tasks are automated may face lower wages or long periods of unemployment. For this reason, debates about automation are increasingly debates about education and social policy.

According to the passage, the textile workers mentioned ----.
c: acted out of fear that machines would endanger their jobs
were the first workers to be retrained for new industries
successfully prevented the spread of industrial machinery
demanded that new sectors be created for unemployed workers
a: Parçada bu işçilerin geçim kaynaklarını tehdit ettiğine inandıkları makineleri tahrip ettikleri belirtiliyor.

s:
The placebo effect, in which patients improve after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, has long been treated by medical researchers as a nuisance to be controlled for rather than a phenomenon worth studying. In clinical trials, a new drug is considered effective only if it performs better than a sugar pill, and any improvement in the placebo group is usually dismissed as noise. In recent decades, however, a growing number of scientists have begun to examine the effect in its own right. Their work suggests that placebo responses are not simply imaginary. Brain imaging studies have shown, for example, that the expectation of pain relief can trigger the release of the body's own pain-reducing chemicals. The strength of the response also appears to depend on context: expensive-looking pills, injections and confident doctors tend to produce larger effects than cheap tablets handed over without explanation. Perhaps most surprisingly, some studies report that patients may benefit even when they are told openly that the pill they are taking contains no medicine. These findings do not mean that placebos can cure serious diseases such as cancer, and researchers stress that the effect is strongest for subjective symptoms like pain, nausea and fatigue. Nevertheless, they raise an important question for medicine: if the way a treatment is delivered influences how well it works, then the doctor's manner and the setting of care may deserve more attention than they currently receive.

According to the passage, placebo effects have traditionally been regarded by medical researchers as ----.
c: something that must be controlled for in drug trials rather than studied
the most reliable method available for measuring how effective a newly developed drug really is
a serious danger to the health of patients who agree to take part in clinical trials
an effective treatment for serious diseases such as cancer
a: Parçanın başında plasebo etkisinin araştırmacılarca uzun süre “incelenmeye değer bir olgu değil, kontrol edilmesi gereken bir sorun (nuisance)” olarak görüldüğü söylenir. Kanseri tedavi ettiği ise açıkça reddedilir.

The placebo effect, in which patients improve after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, has long been treated by medical researchers as a nuisance to be controlled for rather than a phenomenon worth studying. In clinical trials, a new drug is considered effective only if it performs better than a sugar pill, and any improvement in the placebo group is usually dismissed as noise. In recent decades, however, a growing number of scientists have begun to examine the effect in its own right. Their work suggests that placebo responses are not simply imaginary. Brain imaging studies have shown, for example, that the expectation of pain relief can trigger the release of the body's own pain-reducing chemicals. The strength of the response also appears to depend on context: expensive-looking pills, injections and confident doctors tend to produce larger effects than cheap tablets handed over without explanation. Perhaps most surprisingly, some studies report that patients may benefit even when they are told openly that the pill they are taking contains no medicine. These findings do not mean that placebos can cure serious diseases such as cancer, and researchers stress that the effect is strongest for subjective symptoms like pain, nausea and fatigue. Nevertheless, they raise an important question for medicine: if the way a treatment is delivered influences how well it works, then the doctor's manner and the setting of care may deserve more attention than they currently receive.

It can be inferred from the passage that the author believes ----.
c: doctors' behaviour and the care setting could play a bigger role in treatment than is usually assumed
placebos should gradually replace conventional medicines, especially for patients who suffer from chronic pain
brain imaging studies have proved that placebo responses exist only in the patient's imagination
patients should never be told that they are receiving a placebo

Plasebonun ilaçların yerini alması önerilmez; beyin görüntüleme etkinin hayali olmadığını gösterir; açıkça söylenen plasebonun da işe yarayabileceği belirtilir.

s:
When Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable metal type in Mainz around 1450, he could hardly have foreseen how quickly the technology would spread. Within roughly fifty years, printing presses were operating in more than two hundred European towns, and millions of books had been produced. Historians have long debated the consequences of this transformation. One traditional view holds that printing led directly to mass literacy, but this claim is difficult to sustain. Books remained expensive for decades, and in most regions the majority of the population still could not read well into the eighteenth century. What printing did change, almost immediately, was the speed and uniformity with which ideas circulated among those who were already literate. Before print, a text copied by hand could differ significantly from one copy to the next, as scribes introduced errors or made deliberate changes. Printed editions, by contrast, allowed scholars in different cities to refer to the same page of the same text, which made it far easier to compare, criticise and build upon one another's work. Some historians argue that this shared reference point was a precondition for the rapid scientific exchanges of later centuries. Printing also played a decisive role in religious and political debates, since pamphlets could be produced cheaply and distributed widely within weeks. In this sense, the press may have transformed public life less by teaching people to read than by changing what readers could do with texts.

According to the passage, the idea that printing quickly produced mass literacy ----.
c: is hard to defend, since many people remained unable to read for centuries
has been confirmed by most of the historians who have studied the economic and social life of the period
explains why books became cheap soon after Gutenberg's invention
was first suggested by scholars in the eighteenth century

s:
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support an extraordinary share of marine life, providing food and shelter for roughly a quarter of all known marine species. The corals that build these reefs live in a close partnership with tiny algae that inhabit their tissues. The algae produce food through photosynthesis and pass much of it to the coral, while also giving reefs their bright colours. This relationship, however, is sensitive to temperature. When the water becomes unusually warm for several weeks, the partnership breaks down and the corals expel the algae, leaving their white skeletons visible through transparent tissue. This process, known as bleaching, does not kill corals immediately, but without their algae they are starved of most of their energy. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can regain their algae and recover; if the heat lasts too long, large areas of reef may die. Scientists have recorded several mass bleaching events across the world's tropical oceans in recent decades, and they warn that such events are becoming more frequent as sea temperatures rise. A reef that bleaches every two or three years may never have enough time to recover fully. Efforts to protect reefs therefore include reducing local pressures such as pollution and overfishing, which can make corals more resilient, as well as experimental projects to breed corals that tolerate heat better.

According to the passage, coral bleaching occurs when ----.
c: prolonged warm water causes corals to expel the algae living in their tissues
the algae living in coral tissues begin to grow too quickly and eventually cover the whole surface of the coral
overfishing removes the species that feed on algae
corals produce too much food through photosynthesis

s:
Classical economic theory assumed that people make decisions by weighing costs and benefits in a consistent way. If losing a hundred dollars makes someone exactly as unhappy as gaining a hundred dollars makes them happy, then their choices should be predictable and stable. Beginning in the 1970s, however, the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed through a series of experiments that real human behaviour departs from this model in systematic ways. One of their best-known findings is loss aversion: for most people, the pain of losing something is considerably stronger than the pleasure of gaining something of equal value. As a result, people will often reject a bet that offers an even chance of winning or losing the same amount of money, even though, on average, they would lose nothing by accepting it. Loss aversion also helps to explain why investors tend to hold on to falling shares for too long, hoping to avoid admitting a loss, and why people value objects they own more highly than identical objects they do not own. Such findings contributed to the rise of behavioural economics, a field that combines insights from psychology with economic analysis. Critics have pointed out that the size of loss aversion varies between studies and situations, and that some laboratory results may not hold in real markets. Even so, the idea that losses loom larger than gains is now widely accepted as an important feature of human decision-making.

According to the passage, loss aversion means that people ----.
c: feel the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain
always accept bets that offer them an equal chance of winning or losing the same amount of money
value the objects belonging to other people more highly than identical objects they own themselves
make decisions exactly as classical economic theory predicts

s:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, a large proportion are considered endangered, and linguists estimate that many of them may stop being spoken within this century. A language rarely disappears because its speakers suddenly abandon it. More often, the process is gradual: parents who speak a minority language begin to raise their children in a more widely used language, believing that it will offer them better opportunities in education and employment. The children may still understand the language of their grandparents, but they rarely use it, and their own children may not learn it at all. When the last fluent speakers die, the language disappears with them, together with knowledge that may not exist anywhere else, such as names for local plants, traditional stories and ways of describing the world. In response, communities and researchers have developed a range of revitalisation efforts. These include recording elderly speakers, producing dictionaries and teaching materials, and creating schools in which children are taught through the endangered language. Some projects have been remarkably successful. Hebrew, for instance, which for centuries was used mainly in religious and written contexts, became the everyday language of millions of people in the twentieth century. Such cases are exceptional, however, and most experts agree that revival is possible only when a community itself is strongly committed to using the language in daily life.

According to the passage, languages usually become endangered because ----.
c: parents gradually stop passing them on to their children in favour of more widely used languages
speakers suddenly decide, often within a single generation, that they no longer want to use them at all
linguists fail to record them before the last speakers die
governments ban them from being taught in schools

s:
The discovery of antibiotics in the twentieth century transformed medicine, turning infections that had once been fatal into conditions that could be treated within days. Almost from the beginning, however, scientists warned that bacteria would fight back. Because bacteria reproduce very rapidly, random genetic changes appear frequently in large populations. When an antibiotic is used, it kills the bacteria that are sensitive to it, but any that happen to carry a change allowing them to survive are left to multiply. Over time, the resistant strain can become dominant. Bacteria can also pass genes for resistance directly to one another, sometimes even between different species, which allows resistance to spread faster than mutation alone would permit. Human behaviour has accelerated this natural process. Antibiotics are often prescribed for viral illnesses such as colds, against which they have no effect, and patients sometimes stop taking their medicine as soon as they feel better, allowing the hardiest bacteria to survive. In many countries, large quantities of antibiotics are also given to farm animals to promote growth or prevent disease. Health organisations now describe antimicrobial resistance as one of the most serious threats to global health, since routine operations and treatments such as chemotherapy depend on the ability to prevent and treat infections. Meanwhile, relatively few new classes of antibiotics have been developed in recent decades, partly because such drugs are less profitable for pharmaceutical companies than medicines that patients take for many years.

According to the passage, using an antibiotic can lead to resistance because ----.
c: it leaves alive the bacteria that already carry changes allowing them to survive
it causes all of the bacteria in a population to develop new resistance genes immediately
it makes bacteria reproduce more slowly than before
it prevents bacteria from sharing genes with one another
a: Antibiyotik duyarlı bakterileri öldürür; ancak hayatta kalmalarını sağlayan bir değişikliğe zaten sahip olanlar çoğalmaya devam eder ve zamanla dirençli suş baskın hâle gelir.

When large numbers of office workers began working from home, managers and researchers were eager to know whether productivity would rise or fall. The evidence so far suggests that there is no simple answer. Several studies have found that employees working remotely complete as much work as their colleagues in the office, or even more, partly because they spend less time commuting and are interrupted less often. Other research, however, points to costs that are harder to measure. Workers at home tend to communicate mainly with people they already know well, and they have fewer of the informal conversations through which new ideas often emerge. Younger employees may also find it harder to learn from experienced colleagues when they cannot observe them at work. The type of task appears to matter a great deal. Work that requires long periods of concentration, such as writing a report or analysing data, often benefits from the quiet of a home office, while tasks that depend on close collaboration or creative brainstorming may suffer. For this reason, many organisations have settled on hybrid arrangements, in which employees spend some days in the office and others at home. Supporters argue that this combines the advantages of both, although critics note that it can also combine their disadvantages if teams do not coordinate which days they come in, so that people travel to the office only to spend the day on video calls.

According to the passage, one reason remote workers may be more productive is that they ----.
c: are interrupted less often and do not lose time commuting
communicate more often with colleagues they did not know well before working from home
learn more quickly from experienced colleagues
have more informal conversations that create new ideas

s:
When large numbers of office workers began working from home, managers and researchers were eager to know whether productivity would rise or fall. The evidence so far suggests that there is no simple answer. Several studies have found that employees working remotely complete as much work as their colleagues in the office, or even more, partly because they spend less time commuting and are interrupted less often. Other research, however, points to costs that are harder to measure. Workers at home tend to communicate mainly with people they already know well, and they have fewer of the informal conversations through which new ideas often emerge. Younger employees may also find it harder to learn from experienced colleagues when they cannot observe them at work. The type of task appears to matter a great deal. Work that requires long periods of concentration, such as writing a report or analysing data, often benefits from the quiet of a home office, while tasks that depend on close collaboration or creative brainstorming may suffer. For this reason, many organisations have settled on hybrid arrangements, in which employees spend some days in the office and others at home. Supporters argue that this combines the advantages of both, although critics note that it can also combine their disadvantages if teams do not coordinate which days they come in, so that people travel to the office only to spend the day on video calls.

The author suggests that the effect of remote work on productivity ----.
c: depends largely on the kind of task being done
is always negative for tasks requiring concentration
has been measured precisely by most studies
is the same for younger and older employees
a: “The type of task appears to matter a great deal” cümlesiyle verimlilik etkisinin büyük ölçüde işin türüne bağlı olduğu söylenir. Yoğun konsantrasyon gerektiren işler evde genellikle fayda görür.

s:
In April 1815, Mount Tambora on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted in what is considered the most powerful volcanic eruption in recorded history. Tens of thousands of people on the island and nearby areas died, either directly or from the famine and disease that followed. The effects, however, extended far beyond the region. The eruption threw enormous amounts of sulphur gas high into the atmosphere, where it formed a fine layer of particles that reflected part of the sun's light back into space. Over the following year, average temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere fell noticeably. In 1816, which became known in Europe and North America as the "Year Without a Summer", snow fell in parts of New England in June, and cold, wet weather destroyed crops across much of Western Europe. Food prices rose sharply, and hunger contributed to social unrest and migration. Interestingly, people at the time had little idea that these disasters were connected to an eruption on the other side of the world; the link was established by scientists much later. The episode is now frequently studied by climate researchers, because it shows how quickly a change in the composition of the atmosphere can affect weather and food supplies on a global scale. It has also been cited in discussions of proposals to cool the planet artificially by releasing particles into the upper atmosphere, a strategy whose risks remain highly controversial.

According to the passage, the eruption of Tambora caused temperatures to fall because ----.
c: particles formed in the atmosphere reflected some sunlight back into space
huge amounts of volcanic ash fell on the fields of Western Europe and North America
the eruption changed the direction of ocean currents
thick clouds of smoke completely blocked out the sun's light for several months

s:
For much of the twentieth century, raising children with two languages was widely believed to be harmful. Educators and some psychologists warned that bilingual children would become confused, fall behind in school, or fail to master either language properly. Later research largely overturned this view. Studies found that bilingual children may know fewer words in each individual language than monolingual children of the same age, but that their total vocabulary across both languages is usually similar, and that any delay in one language tends to disappear over time. More controversially, some researchers proposed that bilingualism brings cognitive advantages. Because bilingual people must constantly keep one language active while suppressing the other, they argued, they develop stronger executive control, the set of mental skills used to focus attention and switch between tasks. Early experiments appeared to support this claim, and it received considerable attention in the media. In recent years, however, several large studies have failed to find consistent differences between bilingual and monolingual participants on such tasks, and some researchers suspect that studies reporting an advantage were more likely to be published than those that did not. The debate is far from settled. What is clear, according to most specialists, is that bilingualism does not harm children's development, and that its practical benefits, such as the ability to communicate with more people and access different cultures, are reason enough to value it.

According to the passage, research on bilingual children's vocabulary has shown that ----.
c: their combined vocabulary in both languages is usually similar to that of monolingual children
they always know more words in each of their languages than monolingual children of the same age
they never catch up with monolingual children in either language
they become confused and fail to learn either language properly
a: Araştırmalar iki dilli çocukların her bir dilde daha az kelime bilebileceğini, ancak iki dildeki toplam kelime dağarcıklarının genellikle tek dilli akranlarıyla benzer olduğunu ve gecikmenin zamanla kaybolduğunu buldu.

s:
Honeybees are often presented as the most important pollinators of crops, and in many farming systems they do play a central role. Large numbers of hives are transported from farm to farm to pollinate fruit trees and other crops during their short flowering seasons. However, ecologists increasingly emphasise that wild insects, including thousands of species of solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and beetles, are also essential. Some studies have found that wild pollinators improve the quantity and quality of fruit even on farms where honeybees are abundant, apparently because different insects visit flowers at different times of day, in different weather conditions, or in different ways. Bumblebees, for example, can fly in cooler and windier weather than honeybees, and some plants release their pollen only when a flower is vibrated by a buzzing insect, a technique honeybees do not use. Unlike honeybees, which are managed by beekeepers, wild pollinators depend entirely on the surrounding landscape for food and nesting sites. Intensive agriculture, the loss of hedges and wildflower meadows, and the use of certain pesticides have all contributed to declines in many wild species. Interest in urban beekeeping has grown in many cities, and while this can raise public awareness, some researchers warn that adding large numbers of honeybee hives to small green areas may increase competition for flowers and leave less food for wild bees. Protecting pollination, they argue, depends more on planting diverse flowers and preserving habitats than on keeping more hives.

According to the passage, wild pollinators can improve fruit production even where honeybees are common because ----.
c: different insects visit flowers in different conditions and in different ways
wild insects are regularly transported from one farm to another by beekeepers during the flowering season
honeybees avoid flowers that have already been visited
wild insects produce more honey than honeybees
a: Parçaya göre farklı böcekler çiçekleri günün farklı saatlerinde, farklı hava koşullarında ya da farklı biçimlerde ziyaret eder; bu yüzden bal arısı bol olsa bile yabani tozlayıcılar meyve miktarını ve kalitesini artırır.

Parents of teenagers often complain that their children stay up late and are almost impossible to wake in the morning. It is tempting to blame this on laziness or on the attractions of mobile phones, but research suggests that biology plays a significant role. During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts, so that the hormone melatonin, which helps to bring on sleep, is released later in the evening than in childhood. As a result, many adolescents simply do not feel sleepy until late at night. Their need for sleep, however, does not decrease; most experts recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night. When school starts early, many of them are forced to get up long before their bodies are ready, and they accumulate a significant sleep debt over the week. This has been linked to poorer concentration, lower academic performance, mood problems and an increased risk of accidents among young drivers. Several school districts that have experimented with later start times have reported that students sleep longer, attend classes more regularly and are less likely to fall asleep in lessons. Changing school schedules is not simple, though, since it affects transport, parents' working hours and after-school activities. Screens and evening habits also matter: bright light from devices late at night can delay sleep further, which is why researchers recommend combining later start times with better sleep habits at home.

According to the passage, teenagers often go to sleep late because ----.
c: their internal clock shifts so that melatonin is released later in the evening
they need considerably less sleep than younger children once they have reached puberty
they are naturally lazier than adults
schools begin later than they did in the past
a: Ergenlikte iç saat kayar ve uykuyu getiren melatonin hormonu çocukluğa göre akşam daha geç salgılanır; bu yüzden birçok genç gece geç saate kadar uykulu hissetmez. Uyku ihtiyaçları ise azalmaz.

s:
Plastic does not biodegrade in the way that wood or paper does. Instead, exposure to sunlight, waves and changes in temperature gradually breaks larger items into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces smaller than five millimetres are usually described as microplastics, and they are now found almost everywhere scientists look: in deep ocean sediments, Arctic ice, agricultural soils, drinking water and the air of cities. Some microplastics are produced deliberately at a small size, such as the tiny beads once commonly added to cosmetics, but most result from the breakdown of bottles, bags, fishing nets and synthetic clothing, which releases fibres when it is washed. Because microplastics are so small, they can be eaten by plankton and other small organisms at the base of the food chain, and they have been detected in fish, shellfish and, increasingly, in human tissues. What remains uncertain is how harmful they are. Laboratory studies have shown that high concentrations can damage the health of some marine animals, and that plastic particles can carry chemicals added during manufacturing or absorbed from the environment. For humans, however, the evidence is still limited, partly because measuring very small particles accurately is technically difficult and because people are exposed to many other substances at the same time. Scientists therefore call for more research, while many argue that, given how persistent plastic is, it would be sensible to reduce plastic pollution without waiting for definitive proof of harm.

According to the passage, most microplastics ----.
c: come from the breakdown of larger plastic products
are manufactured deliberately for use in cosmetics
are produced by plankton at the base of the food chain
disappear completely after a few years in the ocean
a: Bazı mikroplastikler bilerek küçük üretilir (kozmetiklerdeki boncuklar gibi), ancak çoğu şişe, poşet, balık ağı ve sentetik giysi gibi daha büyük ürünlerin parçalanmasından oluşur.

The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of overland and sea routes that connected China with Central Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe for well over a thousand years. Few merchants ever travelled its entire length. Instead, goods usually passed from one trader to another, changing hands many times in the markets and caravan stops along the way. Chinese silk, which gave the network its name in the nineteenth century, was certainly an important product, but the routes also carried spices, precious metals, glassware, horses, paper and countless other items. Equally significant was the exchange of ideas and technologies. Buddhism travelled from India into Central Asia and China along these routes, and later Islam spread eastward through the same networks. Techniques for making paper moved westward from China, eventually reaching the Islamic world and then Europe, where they contributed to profound changes in the recording and spread of knowledge. Not everything that travelled was beneficial, however. Historians believe that the plague known as the Black Death, which killed a large proportion of Europe's population in the fourteenth century, spread partly along trade routes connecting Asia and Europe. The history of the Silk Road is therefore often used to illustrate a broader point: that long-distance connections between societies bring both opportunities and risks, a lesson that seems highly relevant in today's globalised world.

s:
The human digestive system is home to trillions of microorganisms, most of them bacteria, which together are known as the gut microbiome. For a long time these microbes received little attention, apart from the few that cause disease. Advances in genetic sequencing, however, have made it possible to identify thousands of species that cannot easily be grown in a laboratory, and research into the microbiome has expanded dramatically. It is now clear that gut bacteria perform many useful functions. They help to break down dietary fibre that human enzymes cannot digest, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the intestine; they produce certain vitamins; and they appear to play a role in training the immune system. Differences in the composition of the microbiome have been associated with a wide range of conditions, including obesity, inflammatory bowel disease and even some mental health problems. Such findings have generated great excitement, and the market for probiotic supplements has grown accordingly. Many scientists, however, urge caution. Most of the studies show associations rather than causes: it is often unclear whether a particular microbiome contributes to a disease or is simply a consequence of it. Moreover, the microbiome varies greatly from person to person, which makes it difficult to define what a healthy one looks like. Diet appears to be one of the strongest influences, and a varied diet rich in fibre is generally considered beneficial, but claims that specific products can reliably improve health should be treated with scepticism.

c: genetic sequencing has made it possible to identify species that are hard to grow in laboratories

a: Genetik dizilemedeki ilerlemeler laboratuvarda kolayca üretilemeyen binlerce türün tanımlanmasını mümkün kıldı ve mikrobiyom araştırmaları bu sayede hızla genişledi.

s:
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner tested an idea that had circulated among country people for some time: that milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a mild disease of cattle, seemed to be protected from smallpox, one of the deadliest diseases of the age. Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and introduced it into a scratch on the arm of a young boy. Some weeks later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy did not become ill. Experiments of this kind would be considered deeply unethical today, but Jenner's work laid the foundation for vaccination; the word itself comes from vacca, the Latin for cow. The practice spread quickly across Europe and beyond, although it also met strong resistance. Some critics objected on religious grounds, others feared that being injected with material from animals would cause strange side effects, and cartoons of the time showed vaccinated people growing cow-like features. Over the following century and a half, vaccination campaigns gradually reduced smallpox in many countries. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified global programme to eliminate the disease, relying on careful surveillance and the vaccination of everyone around each new case. The last naturally occurring case was recorded in 1977, and in 1980 smallpox was officially declared eradicated, the first human disease to be eliminated in this way.

According to the passage, Jenner's experiment was based on the observation that ----.
c: people who had caught cowpox seemed to be protected from smallpox
smallpox was a mild disease that mainly affected cattle
milkmaids were more likely than other people living in the countryside to die of smallpox
children could not catch smallpox from adults
a: Jenner, kırsal kesimde dolaşan bir gözleme dayandı: inek çiçeğine (cowpox) yakalanmış sağımcı kızlar çiçek hastalığından korunmuş görünüyordu.

s:
Is false information spread more widely online than true information? A large study published in 2018 attempted to answer this question by analysing more than a hundred thousand news stories that had been shared on Twitter over roughly a decade and had been checked by independent fact-checking organisations. The researchers found that false stories reached more people, and did so faster, than true ones. Perhaps surprisingly, automated accounts, or bots, did not explain the difference: when bot activity was removed from the analysis, false news still spread further, suggesting that human users were largely responsible. The authors proposed that novelty may be part of the explanation. False stories tended to be more surprising than true ones, and people may be more inclined to share information that seems new, partly because doing so makes them appear well informed. Replies to false stories also expressed more surprise and disgust, emotions that may encourage sharing. The study has been widely cited, although other researchers have noted that its findings apply to stories that were checked by fact-checkers, which may not be representative of all the news people encounter. Nevertheless, the results have influenced discussions about how platforms and users might respond to misinformation. Some proposals focus on removing false content, while others emphasise simple measures that encourage people to consider whether a story is accurate before they share it.

According to the study described in the passage, false news spread further than true news ----.
c: even when the activity of automated accounts was excluded
only because automated accounts shared it far more often than human users did
because it was less surprising than true news
a: Bot etkinliği analizden çıkarıldığında bile yanlış haberlerin daha geniş yayıldığı bulundu; yani farkın sorumlusu büyük ölçüde insan kullanıcılardı.

s:
Mountain glaciers are sometimes described as natural water towers. During cold seasons they store water as ice, and during warm, dry months they release it gradually as meltwater, feeding rivers on which millions of people depend for drinking water, farming and electricity. In parts of Asia and South America in particular, glacier melt can make up a significant share of river flow in late summer, when rain is scarce. Most of the world's mountain glaciers are now shrinking as temperatures rise. In the short term, this can actually increase the amount of water flowing in rivers, because more ice is melting each year than before. Scientists warn, however, that this increase is temporary. As glaciers become smaller, the amount of meltwater they can provide eventually reaches a peak and then declines, a point sometimes called "peak water". Some smaller glaciers have probably already passed this point. For communities downstream, the consequences could be serious, particularly in dry seasons, when glacier melt has traditionally helped to maintain river levels. Retreating glaciers can also create hazards, such as lakes held back by unstable piles of rock and ice, which may burst suddenly and cause floods. Adapting to these changes may require new reservoirs, more efficient irrigation and careful planning of water use, measures that are costly and that must often be coordinated between countries sharing the same rivers.

According to the passage, glaciers are described as natural water towers because ----.
c: they store water as ice and release it slowly during warm, dry periods
they produce most of the rain and snow that falls on mountain regions during the year
they prevent rivers from flooding during the rainy season
they are used directly to generate electricity

s:
The octopus has long fascinated biologists because it appears to combine remarkable intelligence with a body plan completely unlike our own. Octopuses have been observed solving puzzles, opening jars to reach food, escaping from tanks and, in the wild, carrying coconut shells to use as portable shelters. Such behaviour is all the more striking because the octopus belongs to the molluscs, the same group as snails and clams, and its last common ancestor with vertebrates lived hundreds of millions of years ago. Whatever intelligence the octopus possesses must therefore have evolved largely independently of ours. Its nervous system is also organised differently. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of some mammals, but roughly two thirds of them are located not in the brain but in the arms. Each arm appears to be able to process information and control its own movements to a considerable degree, which has led some researchers to describe the animal as having a highly distributed form of intelligence. The octopus's short life adds another puzzle. Most species live only one or two years, and the young receive no care from their parents, so they cannot learn by observing adults. Some scientists suggest that intelligence may have evolved in octopuses because the loss of a protective shell, which their ancestors once had, made them vulnerable and forced them to rely on flexibility and problem-solving to find food and avoid predators.

According to the passage, octopus intelligence is particularly interesting because ----.
c: it seems to have evolved largely independently of vertebrate intelligence
octopuses are closely related to mammals
octopuses learn most of their problem-solving skills by observing their parents in the wild
it is located entirely in the octopus's brain
a: Ahtapot yumuşakçalardandır ve omurgalılarla son ortak ataları yüz milyonlarca yıl önce yaşamıştır; bu yüzden zekâsı büyük ölçüde bizimkinden bağımsız evrimleşmiş olmalıdır.

Few questions in economics provoke as much public debate as the effect of minimum wages on employment. The traditional textbook argument is straightforward: if the government requires employers to pay more than the market wage, employers will hire fewer workers, so a higher minimum wage may help those who keep their jobs but harm those who lose them or never find one. For decades this prediction was widely accepted. In the early 1990s, however, a well-known study compared fast-food restaurants in two neighbouring American states, one of which had just raised its minimum wage, and found no evidence that employment had fallen in the state with the higher wage. The study triggered a long and sometimes heated debate. Critics questioned its data and methods, while supporters argued that in many local labour markets employers have enough power to set wages below the level that competition would produce, in which case a moderate minimum wage need not reduce employment. Since then, a large body of research has accumulated. Many economists now believe that moderate increases have small effects on employment, while acknowledging that very large increases, especially in regions where average wages are low, could still lead to job losses. Researchers also study other ways in which employers may respond, such as raising prices, reducing working hours or investing in automation. The debate continues, but it has become less about whether minimum wages destroy jobs in principle and more about how high they can be set without doing so.

c: may lead employers to hire fewer workers

has no effect on employers' decisions
benefits only workers who lose their jobs

Ancient Roman concrete has puzzled engineers for a long time. Many Roman harbours, bridges and buildings have survived for around two thousand years, while modern concrete structures often begin to crack and decay within decades. The Romans did not use modern cement; instead they mixed lime with volcanic ash, which reacts with the lime to form a strong binding material. In structures built in the sea, seawater seeping into the concrete appears to have encouraged the growth of new minerals in cracks and pores, gradually strengthening the material rather than weakening it. More recent research has drawn attention to small white lumps of lime that are commonly found in Roman concrete. These were long thought to be signs of careless mixing, but some scientists now argue that they were a consequence of the way the Romans prepared their mixture and that they may have helped the material repair itself. According to this theory, when water enters a crack, it dissolves part of the lime, which can then form new mineral crystals that fill the gap. Researchers caution that Roman concrete is not simply better than modern concrete: it is weaker under heavy loads and takes longer to harden, which makes it unsuitable for many modern purposes. Nevertheless, understanding why it lasts so long could help engineers design more durable materials, and since the production of modern cement is responsible for a significant share of global carbon dioxide emissions, longer-lasting concrete could also benefit the environment.

According to the passage, Roman marine structures may have become stronger over time because ----.
c: seawater encouraged the growth of new minerals in cracks and pores

volcanic ash prevented any seawater from entering the concrete through cracks and pores
they were built only in areas with calm water

In the mid-1980s, British scientists working in Antarctica reported that the amount of ozone above the continent fell dramatically every spring. The ozone layer, located high in the stratosphere, absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation, so the discovery of this "ozone hole" caused considerable alarm. Researchers soon identified the main cause: chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, synthetic chemicals widely used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays. Once released, CFCs rise slowly into the stratosphere, where sunlight breaks them apart and frees chlorine, which destroys ozone molecules. The extreme cold over Antarctica in winter creates conditions in which this destruction becomes especially rapid when sunlight returns in spring. The international response was unusually swift. In 1987 governments agreed on the Montreal Protocol, which committed countries to phasing out the production of CFCs and related substances, and the agreement was later strengthened several times. Because these chemicals remain in the atmosphere for decades, the ozone layer could not recover immediately. Recent assessments, however, indicate that it is gradually healing, and that the Antarctic ozone hole may return to its 1980 condition around the 2060s if current policies are maintained. The Montreal Protocol is frequently cited as one of the most successful environmental agreements ever made, and observers often ask what lessons it might offer for tackling climate change, though they also note that replacing CFCs was a far simpler task than transforming the world's energy systems.

According to the passage, CFCs damage the ozone layer because ----.
c: sunlight breaks them apart in the stratosphere and releases chlorine that destroys ozone
they absorb most of the ultraviolet radiation before it can reach the ozone layer
they make the air above Antarctica extremely cold in winter
they react with water inside refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays
a: CFC'ler stratosfere yükselir; orada güneş ışığı onları parçalar ve ozon moleküllerini yok eden klor açığa çıkar.

s:
Eyewitness testimony has traditionally been regarded as one of the most persuasive forms of evidence in criminal trials. A confident witness who says, "That is the man I saw," can strongly influence a jury. Yet decades of psychological research have shown that human memory is far less reliable than most people assume. Memory does not work like a video recording that can simply be replayed. Instead, each time an event is remembered, it is partly reconstructed, and this process makes it vulnerable to distortion. In a series of famous experiments beginning in the 1970s, the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed participants films of car accidents and then asked them questions about what they had seen. When the question was phrased using the word "smashed" rather than "hit", participants estimated higher speeds, and some later reported seeing broken glass that had not been in the film. Other studies have shown that misleading information introduced after an event can become incorporated into a person's memory, and that confidence often grows each time a memory is recalled, regardless of its accuracy. These findings have practical consequences. In the United States, reviews of cases in which convicted people were later cleared by DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in a large proportion of them. As a result, many police departments have changed their procedures, for example by ensuring that the officer conducting an identification does not know which person is the suspect, and by recording a witness's level of confidence immediately.

According to the passage, memory is vulnerable to distortion because ----.
c: it is partly reconstructed each time it is recalled
it works in exactly the same way as a video recording that can be replayed
people forget events completely after a few days
a: Parçaya göre bellek video kaydı gibi çalışmaz; her hatırlandığında kısmen yeniden kurulur ve bu süreç onu çarpıtmaya açık hâle getirir.

s:
Artificial light at night has transformed human life, extending working hours and making streets safer. However, ecologists are increasingly concerned about its effects on other species. Many animals rely on natural patterns of light and darkness to regulate their behaviour. Migrating birds that travel at night, for example, can become disoriented by brightly lit buildings and may circle them until they are exhausted or collide with windows. Newly hatched sea turtles normally find their way to the ocean by moving towards the brighter horizon over the water, but lights from beachfront roads and hotels can lead them inland instead. Insects are affected too. Many nocturnal insects are attracted to street lamps, where large numbers die from exhaustion or are eaten by predators, and some researchers believe that light pollution may be one of several factors contributing to declines in insect populations. Because insects pollinate plants and serve as food for birds and bats, such losses can have wider consequences. Unlike many environmental problems, light pollution can be reduced relatively quickly. Measures include directing lights downwards rather than into the sky, switching off unnecessary lighting late at night, and using warmer-coloured lights, which appear to attract fewer insects than bright white or blue light. Some cities have introduced such policies, and a number of areas have been officially recognised as "dark sky" places, where artificial light is carefully controlled to protect wildlife and allow people to see the stars.

According to the passage, newly hatched sea turtles can be misled by artificial light because ----.
c: they normally move towards the brightest horizon to reach the sea
they are attracted by the warmth coming from hotel buildings and beachfront roads
they hunt insects that gather around street lamps
they need darkness in order to hatch
a: Yeni çıkan deniz kaplumbağaları normalde denizin üzerindeki daha parlak ufka doğru giderek okyanusu bulur; sahil yolları ve otellerin ışıkları onları karaya doğru yönlendirebilir.

s:
Until recently, the story of human origins was reconstructed mainly from fossils and stone tools. Over the past two decades, however, the ability to extract and sequence DNA from ancient bones has revolutionised the field. One of the most striking discoveries concerns our relationship with the Neanderthals, a group of humans who lived in Europe and western Asia until around forty thousand years ago. Many scientists once believed that Neanderthals and modern humans had not interbred. Yet when the Neanderthal genome was sequenced, researchers found that people of non-African descent today carry roughly one to two percent Neanderthal DNA, indicating that the two groups did have children together after modern humans spread out of Africa. Analysis of a small finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed another previously unknown group, now called the Denisovans, whose genetic legacy survives particularly in some populations of South-East Asia and Oceania. Some of the genes inherited from these ancient relatives appear to have been useful; a Denisovan variant, for example, is thought to help some Tibetan populations cope with low oxygen levels at high altitude. Ancient DNA has also transformed the study of more recent prehistory, showing that the populations of many regions were reshaped repeatedly by large-scale migrations. Such findings have overturned the idea that present-day groups have lived in the same place, unchanged, since ancient times, and they have made it clear that mixing between populations has been a constant feature of human history.

According to the passage, the sequencing of the Neanderthal genome showed that ----.
c: Neanderthals and modern humans had children together
modern humans and Neanderthals never met each other after leaving Africa
Neanderthals lived in Europe until very recently
a: Neandertal genomu dizilendiğinde Afrika kökenli olmayan bugünkü insanların yaklaşık yüzde bir-iki Neandertal DNA'sı taşıdığı görüldü; bu da iki grubun birlikte çocuk sahibi olduğunu gösterir.

Some of the genes inherited from these ancient relatives appear to have been useful; a Denisovan variant, for example, is thought to help some Tibetan populations cope with low oxygen levels at high altitude. Ancient DNA has also transformed the study of more recent prehistory, showing that the populations of many regions were reshaped repeatedly by large-scale migrations. Most countries today give their central banks the task of keeping inflation low and stable, often aiming for a rate of around two percent a year. The main tool they use is the interest rate at which commercial banks can borrow money from the central bank. When inflation rises above the target, the central bank usually raises this rate. Borrowing then becomes more expensive for banks, which pass the higher cost on to households and businesses through higher interest rates on loans and mortgages. As a result, people tend to spend less and save more, companies postpone investment, and the slowdown in demand eventually reduces the pressure on prices. When the economy is weak and inflation is low, the central bank can do the opposite, lowering rates to encourage borrowing and spending. This mechanism works with considerable delays: economists often estimate that changes in interest rates take a year or more to have their full effect on inflation. Central bankers must therefore make decisions based on forecasts of where the economy is heading, which are inevitably uncertain. Why do many economists believe that central banks should be independent of governments? The main argument is that politicians may be tempted to keep interest rates low before elections to boost the economy in the short term, even if this leads to higher inflation later. Independence is intended to protect monetary policy from such pressures, although critics argue that it gives considerable power to officials who are not elected.

c: loans become more expensive and demand in the economy tends to slow down
companies immediately increase their investment in new equipment and buildings
inflation rises above the target rate
households are encouraged to borrow more money and increase their spending

In 1906 the scientist Francis Galton visited a country fair in England where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and prepared. Galton, who was sceptical of the abilities of ordinary people, collected around eight hundred guesses after the contest. To his surprise, the middle value of all the guesses was within one percent of the true weight, closer than most individual estimates. This episode is often cited as an early example of what has come to be called the "wisdom of crowds": under certain conditions, the combined judgement of a large group can be more accurate than that of most of its members, including experts. The explanation is statistical. Each individual guess contains some error, but if people's errors are independent of one another, overestimates and underestimates tend to cancel out when the guesses are combined. The important phrase, however, is "under certain conditions". The effect depends on people having some relevant knowledge, on a diversity of views, and above all on independence. If members of a group influence one another, for example by hearing each other's opinions before giving their own, their errors may become correlated, and the group can confidently converge on a wrong answer. This helps to explain why committees sometimes make poorer decisions than their members would have made alone, and why some organisations ask people to record their estimates privately before any discussion begins.

What surprised Galton about the guesses he collected at the fair?
c: Their combined middle value was very close to the actual weight of the ox.
Most visitors guessed the weight of the ox exactly.
Experts' guesses were much more accurate than those of the ordinary visitors to the fair.
Nobody was able to guess the weight within one percent.
a: Galton tahminlerin orta değerinin gerçek ağırlığın yüzde biri kadar yakınında olduğunu, çoğu bireysel tahminden daha isabetli olduğunu gördü ve şaşırdı.

s:
Dyslexia is a common learning difficulty that mainly affects the ability to read and spell accurately and fluently. It is not related to general intelligence: people with dyslexia can be highly capable in many areas, and many successful scientists, writers and business leaders have described their own experiences of the condition. Research suggests that the central problem for most people with dyslexia lies in processing the sounds of language. To learn to read in a language that uses an alphabet, a child must understand that words are made up of smaller sounds and must link these sounds to letters. Children with dyslexia often find this connection difficult, which makes decoding unfamiliar words slow and effortful. Contrary to a popular belief, seeing letters backwards is not the defining feature of dyslexia; many young children reverse letters such as b and d while they are learning to write, whether or not they have the condition. Dyslexia tends to run in families, and studies of twins indicate that genetic factors play an important role, although no single gene is responsible. Early identification is considered important, because structured teaching that focuses explicitly on the links between sounds and letters can significantly improve reading skills, particularly when it begins in the first years of school. Adjustments such as extra time in examinations and the use of audiobooks or text-to-speech software can also help students to demonstrate their knowledge without being held back by slow reading.

According to the passage, the main difficulty for most people with dyslexia is related to ----.
c: processing the sounds that make up words
understanding the meaning of difficult texts

s:
The term "fast fashion" describes a business model in which clothing companies produce large volumes of inexpensive garments and introduce new styles at a very rapid pace, sometimes every few weeks. By quickly copying trends seen on catwalks and social media, these companies have made fashionable clothes affordable for millions of consumers. The model, however, has attracted growing criticism. The number of garments produced worldwide has risen sharply in recent decades, while the average number of times each item is worn before being thrown away has fallen. Much of the discarded clothing ends up in landfills or is burned, and only a small fraction of textiles is recycled into new clothes, partly because many garments are made from blends of different fibres that are difficult to separate. The production of textiles also uses large amounts of water and chemicals, and synthetic fabrics release microscopic fibres when washed. In addition, critics point to poor working conditions in some of the factories, many of them in developing countries, where clothing is made. The 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza building in Bangladesh, which housed several garment factories and killed more than a thousand workers, drew international attention to safety problems in the industry. In response, some companies have introduced recycling schemes and more transparent supply chains, and second-hand clothing has become increasingly popular. Sceptics argue, though, that such measures will have limited impact as long as the business model depends on persuading consumers to buy ever more clothes.

According to the passage, only a small proportion of textiles is recycled into new clothes partly because ----.
c: many garments are made from mixtures of fibres that are hard to separate
consumers prefer to wear their clothes many times before throwing them away
recycling textiles is banned in most of the developing countries where clothes are made
synthetic fabrics are more expensive than natural ones

s:
As fresh water becomes scarcer in many dry regions, desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, has expanded rapidly. Countries in the Middle East, for example, now rely heavily on desalinated water for drinking, and large plants have also been built in Australia, Spain, Israel and parts of the United States. Early desalination plants mostly worked by heating seawater until it evaporated and then collecting the condensed vapour, a process that required enormous amounts of energy. Today most new plants use reverse osmosis, in which seawater is forced at high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass but block salt. Improvements in membranes and in the recovery of energy from the pressurised water have greatly reduced costs, although desalinated water is still generally more expensive than water taken from rivers or underground sources. Desalination also raises environmental concerns. Plants that run on electricity generated from fossil fuels contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, and the process produces brine, a highly concentrated salt solution that is usually returned to the sea. If brine is not diluted properly, it can harm marine life near the outlet, since it is denser than seawater and tends to sink and spread along the sea floor. The intake pipes that draw in seawater can also trap fish and other organisms. Supporters argue that these problems can be reduced through careful design and the use of renewable energy, while critics contend that, in many places, reducing waste and repairing leaking pipes would be cheaper ways to secure water supplies.

According to the passage, reverse osmosis works by ----.
c: pushing seawater at high pressure through membranes that hold back salt
heating seawater until it evaporates and then collecting the condensed vapour
adding chemicals that cause the salt to separate from the water and sink to the sea floor
mixing seawater with river water to dilute the salt
